User: Review on Advise and Consent (Advise and Consent, Book 1):
- Overall: 5.0
- Review: The New York Times Book Review had an article several weeks ago about this book and made me want to reread it. I probably was a teen when I read it and snippets of it came back to me. There are several points that were so interesting. First, the revisiting of the Communist threat as seen in those days, matched by the feeling that our country had lost the Cold War. Second, identifying some of the major players such as Roosevelt and I think Stevenson. The portrait of Joe McCarthy was fascinating.
Most importantly, it raises issues that are with us today under different garb. How relevant is a person's past in considering them for a position? I read this during the Soutemayer confirmation hearings. Without passing judgment, does it really matter what she said 20 years ago? I also wonder if the Senate is as polite now as it was then, if it ever was so polite.
If one wants a taste of history, this is a must-read if you can find it. The only negative is that there are long sections that are inside Washington that could be removed. A quibble only.

Other Review on One Summer: America, 1927 (Random House Large Print):
- Overall: 4.0
- Review: Bill Bryson's "One Summer: America, 1927" is a thrillingly compulsive read. With dazzling speed and skill, Bryson presents in rapid succession the most important stories and people of 1927. The focal point of the book -- just as he was of that summer -- is Charles Lindbergh, whose solo flight across the Atlantic in the tiny, primitive "Spirit of St. Louis" remains one of the most awe-inspiring feats in aviation history. However, Bryson also finds room to discuss plenty of other celebrities of the time -- Herbert Hoover, Calvin Coolidge, Henry Ford, Sacco and Vanzetti, Al Capone, Jack Dempsey, Babe Ruth. He also presents many now-forgotten but still fascinating people: Wayne B. Wheeler, the chief architect of Prohibition; Ruth Snyder and Judd Gray, the murderous adulterers whose case inspired James M. Cain to write both "The Postman Always Rings Twice" and "Double Indemnity"; Benjamin Strong and Montagu Norman, governors of the Federal Reserve and the Bank of England, whose misguided economic policies were a direct cause of the Great Depression; Charles Levine, flamboyant entrepreneur and con man, who tried to transform the nation's aviation craze into his personal cash cow; and the hapless Carrie Buck, the first victim of enforced-sterilization policies, sacrificed on the altar of eugenics. All of these stories are fascinating...
